rationale: Start with a broad organic gradient at moderate temperature to maximize coverage of the unknown mixture and leave time for strongly retained compounds to elute. The retention and resolution pattern will guide subsequent gradient and temperature optimization.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing how much of the current resolution margin can be traded for speed. Keep temperature and endpoints fixed to isolate the gradient-slope effect.
Test higher temperature to change selectivity in the crowded middle cluster while retaining the fast gradient. This may recover the resolution lost in injection 2 without introducing a time penalty.

An intermediate temperature may separate the middle cluster without causing the near-coelution seen at 60 C. A slightly shallower gradient should provide additional resolution while keeping the last peak near the zero-time-penalty region.

Raise temperature by 5 C to improve separation of the remaining close middle pair while checking the pair that nearly coeluted at 60 C. Keep the gradient unchanged because injection 4 already avoided a time penalty.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a slightly shallower gradient to assess nearby method robustness. This small change should keep the last peak near the zero-time-penalty region while revealing how the two marginally resolved pairs respond.

With the maximum CRF already reached, test a modestly higher starting organic fraction for a faster alternative. This probes initial-composition sensitivity while retaining the temperature that resolved all 10 compounds.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to recover resolution of the close pair in injection 7 while preserving its faster elution. This may provide another maximum-score method with a different balance of critical-pair resolutions.

Further flatten the gradient slightly to lift the remaining critical pair above R = 1.5. Extrapolation from injections 7 and 8 suggests the last peak should remain near 8 minutes, potentially retaining a zero time penalty.

Preserve injection 5’s starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while ending the programmed ramp earlier. Since all peaks previously eluted before this new ramp ends, this should retain the maximum CRF with a lower final organic fraction.

Keep the proven gradient slope while ending the ramp at a still lower organic fraction. The ramp reaches the outlet through 8.65 minutes, after the previously observed last peak at 7.60 minutes, so the maximum-score separation should be preserved.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a compensating shallower gradient to seek more resolution margin around the maximum-score region. This combination may improve the balance between the two critical pairs while keeping the last peak near 8 minutes.

The maximum CRF is already secured; test a lower-temperature selectivity regime for an alternative optimal method. The fast gradient may keep the last peak near 8 minutes while cooling changes separation within the crowded middle cluster.

Explore a faster, higher-organic starting condition at 60 C to test whether the troublesome middle pair separates after an elution-order reversal. The maximum score is already secured, so this run searches for an alternative optimum while checking early-peak crowding.

Lower the starting organic fraction to improve early-pair resolution, and steepen the gradient to probe separation on the reversed-order side of the middle-pair crossover. This tests a substantially faster alternative to the established maximum-score methods.

Test whether a steeper gradient increases selectivity for the remaining close pair in the fast 60 C regime. Monitor the neighboring pair carefully, since its resolution of 1.62 in injection 15 leaves little margin for further compression.
Return to the maximum-score region with a gradient slope between injections 8 and 9. This should balance the two critical-pair resolutions above 1.5 while keeping the last peak below 8 minutes.

Preserve the proven gradient slope through the first nine peaks, then test a lower-organic hold for eluting the final compound. This probes whether the maximum CRF can be retained with a shorter ramp and lower final organic fraction.

Preserve injection 9’s gradient slope and its stronger minimum-resolution margin while lowering the final organic fraction. Because the ramp continues at the outlet until 8.65 minutes, after the previously observed last peak, this should retain the maximum CRF.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 9 to map the maximum-score region. The observed trends suggest both critical pairs should remain above R = 1.5, with the final peak still near the demonstrated zero-time-penalty range.

Probe the shallower-gradient boundary of the maximum-score region while keeping the successful starting composition and temperature. Extrapolation suggests the critical resolutions should remain above 1.5, with the last peak near 8.45 minutes and potentially still free of a time penalty.

Test a gradient slope between injections 20 and 21, both of which achieved the maximum CRF. This should preserve full resolution and zero time penalty while using a lower final organic fraction and shorter programmed ramp.

Test whether a final hold at 50% organic can improve the marginal middle-pair resolution seen with the same gradient slope in injection 8. The hold reaches the outlet at 6.65 minutes, so the middle peaks should remain unchanged; this run primarily maps the final-peak time penalty at the lower endpoint.

Test a slope just shallower than injection 6 while retaining the successful low starting organic fraction. Nearby results suggest full resolution and a last peak near 8 minutes, making this another plausible maximum-score method with a lower final organic fraction.

Use the final injection to probe the time-penalty boundary with a slightly shallower gradient than injection 21, which still fully resolved all peaks. The maximum possible CRF is already secured; this run tests whether that optimal region extends to slightly longer retention.
